title: The Mamluk Sultanate
subtitle: 1250–1517 · The Slave-Soldier Empire, the Mongol Wall and the Cairo of the Sultans

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: A ruling caste, not a dynasty — sultans raised from slavery, the Qalawunid line that came closest to heredity, and the Circassian regime of the Citadel towers

entries.label: Aybak, Shajar al-Durr and the seizure of power
entries.hint: The Bahriyya regiment that murdered the last Ayyubid, Turanshah, put his widow Shajar al-Durr on the throne for some eighty days, then married her to the atabeg Aybak, who ruled as sultan with a child Ayyubid as nominal co-sovereign for form. Aybak killed the Bahri leader Aqtay in 1254, driving Baybars and the other Bahris into exile in Syria; in 1257 Shajar al-Durr had Aybak killed, and was herself beaten to death days later.
entries.note: Ibn Wasil (contemporary, an Ayyubid loyalist) and the later al-Maqrizi ('Suluk') and Ibn Taghribirdi ('al-Nujum al-Zahira'); the chroniclers frame Shajar al-Durr through a hostile lens (Duncan, 'Scholarly Views of Shajar al-Durr', 2000). Cross-references the Ayyubid folio.

entries.label: Qutuz and the road to Ayn Jalut
entries.hint: As the Mongols took Aleppo and Damascus, the vice-sultan Qutuz deposed Aybak's young son, recalled the exiled Bahris, and marched into Palestine. On 3 September 1260 his army — Baybars leading the vanguard — destroyed the Mongol force under Kitbugha at Ayn Jalut in Galilee. On the march home Baybars assassinated Qutuz and was acclaimed sultan in his place.
entries.note: Ibn Abd al-Zahir (Baybars' own secretary and panegyrist — read for that bias), al-Yunini, Baybars al-Mansuri; the Mongol side in later Persian sources. Amitai-Preiss, 'Mongols and Mamluks: The Mamluk-Ilkhanid War 1260–1281' (1995). Cross-references the Abbasid 945–1258 and Ayyubid folios.

entries.label: Baybars — the real founder of the Mamluk state
entries.hint: Baybars built the institution: he installed a refugee Abbasid as caliph in Cairo for legitimacy, rebuilt the army and a war fleet, revived the relay post and a Cairo-to-Euphrates signal system, and appointed a chief qadi for each of the four Sunni schools. He campaigned almost every year — against the Franks, the Mongols, Cilician Armenia, the Assassins and Nubia — and allied with the Golden Horde against the Ilkhanate. He died at Damascus in 1277.
entries.note: Ibn Abd al-Zahir, 'al-Rawd al-Zahir' (the official biography, panegyric); al-Yunini and Baybars al-Mansuri (near-contemporary). Thorau, 'The Lion of Egypt: Sultan Baybars I' (1987). Cross-references the Ayyubid folio's entry on the pre-1250 Bahri regiments.

entries.label: The Qalawunid succession begins
entries.hint: Baybars' two sons were pushed aside within two years by the senior emir Qalawun, who founded the one line that would hold the sultanate, on and off, for a century. He beat a full Ilkhanid invasion at Homs in 1281, took the Hospitaller castle of Marqab (1285) and the city of Tripoli (1289), and built the great madrasa-hospital-mausoleum complex on the main avenue of Cairo.
entries.note: Ibn Abd al-Zahir also served Qalawun ('Tashrif al-Ayyam'); Shafi ibn Ali. Northrup, 'From Slave to Sultan: The Career of al-Mansur Qalawun' (1998).

entries.label: Al-Ashraf Khalil takes Acre
entries.hint: Qalawun's son completed the reduction of the crusader states: Acre stormed in May 1291 after a six-week siege, and Tyre, Sidon, Beirut and Athlit abandoned within weeks. Two centuries of Latin rule on the Syrian mainland were over. He was assassinated by a faction of his own emirs in 1293.
entries.note: Abu al-Fida (an Ayyubid prince of Hama who fought at Acre — eyewitness); the 'Templar of Tyre' on the Frankish side; al-Maqrizi. Little, 'The Fall of Akka in 690/1291', in his collected studies.

entries.label: Al-Nasir Muhammad — three reigns and the apogee
entries.hint: Enthroned at nine and twice deposed by strongmen, al-Nasir Muhammad returned in 1310 to rule in his own name for thirty years: the 1323 peace with the Ilkhanate, a vast building programme, the cadastral survey of 1315, marriage diplomacy with the Mongol and Turkish courts, and a court of unmatched splendour funded by ever-heavier extraction from Egypt and Syria.
entries.note: al-Nuwayri, al-Maqrizi, Ibn al-Dawadari (contemporary). Levanoni, 'A Turning Point in Mamluk History: The Third Reign of al-Nasir Muhammad' (1995), argues his patronage practices undermined the system.

entries.label: The strongmen between al-Nasir's reigns
entries.hint: In the gaps between al-Nasir Muhammad's reigns the throne was held by senior emirs: Kitbugha, a Mongol by origin, deposed amid a famine; Lajin, murdered by his own mamluks; and the Circassian Baybars al-Jashnakir, whose brief rule (1309–10) foreshadowed the later regime before al-Nasir's final return.
entries.note: al-Maqrizi and al-Nuwayri; the period is treated in Irwin, 'The Middle East in the Middle Ages: The Early Mamluk Sultanate 1250–1382' (1986).

entries.label: The sons and grandsons of al-Nasir Muhammad
entries.hint: Twelve members of the family held the throne in forty-one years, most of them minors installed and removed by rival emir factions; the effective rulers were great magnates such as Yalbugha al-Umari and, later, the regents for al-Ashraf Sha'ban. The Black Death struck in the middle of it. The last Qalawunid was set aside by Barquq in 1382.
entries.note: al-Maqrizi, 'Suluk'; Ibn Taghribirdi. The factional politics: Irwin (1986), chs. 8–10.

entries.label: Barquq founds the Circassian regime
entries.hint: A Circassian magnate risen through the regiment quartered in the Citadel towers (burj), Barquq deposed the last Qalawunid, survived a counter-coup and a spell back in the ranks (1389–90), and re-established a sultanate recruited now overwhelmingly from the Circassian Caucasus rather than the Qipchaq steppe. He faced down Timur's first demands.
entries.note: Ibn Taghribirdi (whose father served Barquq); al-Maqrizi. The Bahri-to-Burji shift and its causes: Ayalon, 'The Circassians in the Mamluk Kingdom', JAOS (1949).

entries.label: Faraj and the storm of Timur
entries.hint: Barquq's teenage son inherited a war among the emirs and the onslaught of Timur, who sacked Aleppo and Damascus in 1400–1401. Faraj campaigned repeatedly in Syria against rebel viceroys, was briefly deposed, and was finally caught and executed at Damascus in 1412.
entries.note: Ibn Taghribirdi; al-Maqrizi; Ibn Khaldun's autobiography for the fall of Damascus. Fischel, 'Ibn Khaldun and Tamerlane' (1952).

entries.label: Barsbay — Cyprus and the trade monopolies
entries.hint: Barsbay seized Cyprus in 1426, capturing King Janus and making the island tributary, and forced the spice and sugar trades through crown monopolies at fixed prices — filling the treasury for a decade at the cost of the Karimi merchants and the long-term health of the transit economy. He also fought the Aq Qoyunlu in the north.
entries.note: al-Maqrizi (a contemporary and a critic of the monopolies); Ibn Taghribirdi; al-Sakhawi's biography of Barsbay. Darrag, 'L'Égypte sous le règne de Barsbay' (1961).

entries.label: The mid-century sultans — Jaqmaq, Inal, Khushqadam
entries.hint: A run of elderly emirs elected by their peers: Jaqmaq, who raided Hospitaller Rhodes; Inal, whose reign saw the first serious Mamluk-Ottoman friction over the Karamanids; and Khushqadam. Government was by consensus among the great emirs, the sultan first among equals, the treasury chronically short.
entries.note: Ibn Taghribirdi (a court insider through these reigns); al-Sakhawi. Petry, 'The Civilian Elite of Cairo in the Later Middle Ages' (1981), on how the system worked.

entries.label: Qaytbay — the last strong sultan
entries.hint: A reign of twenty-nine years and relative stability: a long, costly, inconclusive war with the Ottomans over the Taurus frontier (1485–1491), campaigns against the Aq Qoyunlu and the Dulkadirids, and the last great flowering of Mamluk architecture — his madrasa in Cairo, his complex in the Northern Cemetery, and buildings from Alexandria to Mecca. He left the treasury exhausted.
entries.note: Ibn Iyas, 'Bada'i al-Zuhur' (contemporary, and increasingly an eyewitness); al-Sakhawi. Petry, 'Twilight of Majesty: The Reigns of al-Ashraf Qaytbay and Qansuh al-Ghawri' (1993).

entries.label: Al-Ghawri, Tuman Bay and the Ottoman conquest
entries.hint: Qansuh al-Ghawri, elected at about sixty, rebuilt the Citadel's defences and raised a corps of gunners, but marched north in 1516 with an army that still fought as horse-archers. He died on the field at Marj Dabiq when the viceroy of Aleppo defected. His nephew Tuman Bay held Cairo for months, lost at al-Raydaniyya in January 1517, and was hanged by Selim I at the Bab Zuwayla.
entries.note: Ibn Iyas is the eyewitness of the whole collapse — partisan for the Mamluks and bitter about the conquest, but on the spot. Petry, 'Protectors or Praetorians? The Last Mamluk Sultans' (1994); Ottoman side in Celalzade. Cross-references the Abbasid 945–1258 folio.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The wall against the Mongols, the liquidation of Outremer, Timur, the Portuguese in the Indian Ocean, and the Ottoman conquest

entries.label: Ayn Jalut
entries.hint: The Mongol army left to hold Syria after Hulagu withdrew east — reduced further by that withdrawal — was destroyed by Qutuz and Baybars near the spring of Goliath in September 1260. It was the first decisive defeat of a Mongol field force in open battle, and it fixed the Euphrates as the western limit of Mongol power for good.
entries.note: Ibn Abd al-Zahir; al-Yunini; the Mongol dimension in Amitai-Preiss, 'Mongols and Mamluks' (1995), which weighs how much the Mongol withdrawal had already reduced Kitbugha's force. Cross-references the Abbasid 945–1258 and Ayyubid folios.

entries.label: Baybars breaks the Frankish states
entries.hint: A methodical sequence of sieges: Caesarea and Arsuf (1265), Safed (1266), the sack of Antioch (1268, the bloodiest single event of the crusading era), and in 1271 the Templar fortress of Safita and the Hospitaller Krak des Chevaliers. Baybars reduced the crusader interior and slighted much of what he took.
entries.note: Ibn Abd al-Zahir; Baybars' own letter to Bohemond VI after the fall of Antioch is preserved and quoted; the Frankish account in the 'Gestes des Chiprois'. Cross-references the Ayyubid folio.

entries.label: Nubia, Cilician Armenia and the Assassins
entries.hint: Baybars extended Mamluk reach in every direction: the Nizari Ismaili castles of Syria surrendered by 1273, ending the Assassins as an independent power; Cilician Armenia was ravaged for its Mongol alliance and its capital Sis sacked (1266); and a Mamluk army took Dongola in 1276, beginning the long subjection of Christian Nubia and the Nile slave supply.
entries.note: Ibn Abd al-Zahir; the Nubian campaigns in Ibn al-Furat. Daftary, 'The Ismailis' (2007), on the end of the Syrian Nizari state.

entries.label: The Ilkhanid invasions — Homs, Wadi al-Khazandar, Shaqhab
entries.hint: Three more Ilkhanid attempts on Syria: beaten at Homs in 1281; a Mamluk disaster at Wadi al-Khazandar in 1299 that let Ghazan hold Damascus for a hundred days; and the decisive Mamluk victory at Marj al-Suffar (Shaqhab), south of Damascus, in 1303. The frontier war ended with the formal peace of 1323.
entries.note: Baybars al-Mansuri and al-Yunini (contemporary); the Ilkhanid side in Rashid al-Din. Amitai-Preiss, 'Mongols and Mamluks' (1995) and his later articles on the 1299–1303 campaigns.

entries.label: The fall of Acre
entries.hint: Al-Ashraf Khalil stormed Acre after a six-week siege in May 1291; the surviving Franks evacuated Tyre, Sidon, Beirut and Athlit within weeks. Two centuries of Latin Christian rule on the Levantine mainland ended, and the Mamluks razed the coastal cities to deny them to any future crusade — at lasting cost to the coast's own trade.
entries.note: Abu al-Fida (present at the siege); the 'Excidium Aconis' and the 'Templar of Tyre' on the Latin side. Cross-references the Ayyubid and Abbasid 945–1258 folios.

entries.label: The wars of the magnate households
entries.hint: With the Qalawunid sultans reduced to figureheads, real power was fought over by rival households of great emirs — Yalbugha al-Umari, then the rise of Barquq, then the revolt of Mintash and Yalbugha al-Nasiri (1389–90) that briefly unseated him. Factional war among the elite became the normal mode of late-Bahri and Burji politics.
entries.note: al-Maqrizi; Ibn Taghribirdi. The structural analysis in Levanoni (1995) and in Van Steenbergen, 'Order out of Chaos: Patronage, Conflict and Mamluk Socio-Political Culture 1341–1382' (2006).

entries.label: Timur sacks Aleppo and Damascus
entries.hint: Timur crushed the Mamluk garrisons of northern Syria, stormed Aleppo, and took Damascus after a siege during which Ibn Khaldun, trapped inside, was lowered over the wall to negotiate and spent weeks in Timur's camp. The Umayyad Mosque burned; the craftsmen of Damascus — glassmakers, armourers, tilemakers — were deported to Samarqand, ending several Syrian industries.
entries.note: Ibn Khaldun's 'al-Ta'rif' (autobiography, eyewitness) and Ibn Taghribirdi; the Timurid side in Sharaf al-Din Ali Yazdi's 'Zafarnama' (panegyric). Fischel, 'Ibn Khaldun and Tamerlane' (1952).

entries.label: The conquest of Cyprus
entries.hint: In reprisal for Catalan and Genoese piracy staged from Cyprus and a Frankish raid that burned part of the Nile Delta, Barsbay's fleets landed on the island, routed the Lusignan army at Khirokitia, and captured King Janus. Cyprus became a tributary of the Mamluk sultan — a rare Mamluk conquest overseas.
entries.note: al-Maqrizi and Ibn Taghribirdi; the Cypriot chronicle of Leontios Makhairas. The campaign in Fuess, 'Rotting Ships and Razed Harbors' (on Mamluk naval policy), IJMES (2001).

entries.label: The Taurus frontier war with the Ottomans
entries.hint: Six years of fighting in Cilicia over the buffer principality of Dulkadir and the Ramadanids; the Mamluk army under Qaytbay's general Azbak held its ground and even captured Ottoman commanders, and the war closed in a status quo peace. It was the last time the Mamluks fought the Ottomans to a draw.
entries.note: Ibn Iyas; the Ottoman chronicles (Ibn Kemal, Tursun Beg). Har-El, 'Struggle for Domination in the Middle East: The Ottoman-Mamluk War 1485–1491' (1995).

entries.group: The Portuguese in the Indian Ocean
entries.label: Chaul and Diu
entries.hint: A Mamluk battle fleet built at Suez, crewed partly by Ottoman and Venetian gunners and allied with the sultan of Gujarat, beat a Portuguese squadron at Chaul in 1508, killing the viceroy's son. The next year it was annihilated off Diu. The Indian Ocean, and with it the spice route, passed to Portugal.
entries.note: Ibn Iyas; the Portuguese account in João de Barros and the 'Commentaries' of Afonso de Albuquerque. Aubin's articles on the Mamluk-Gujarati fleet; Casale, 'The Ottoman Age of Exploration' (2010), for the aftermath.

entries.label: Marj Dabiq
entries.hint: North of Aleppo the Ottoman army of Selim I — janissary infantry with arquebuses behind a line of chained field guns — broke the Mamluk cavalry charge. Al-Ghawri died on the field, of a stroke in most accounts, as Khayrbak, the viceroy of Aleppo, went over to the Ottomans. All of Syria fell within weeks.
entries.note: Ibn Iyas (eyewitness to the news reaching Cairo); the Ottoman side in Celalzade Mustafa and Ibn Kemal. Ayalon, 'Gunpowder and Firearms in the Mamluk Kingdom' (1956), on why the Mamluk army was out-shot.

entries.label: Al-Raydaniyya and the fall of Cairo
entries.hint: Tuman Bay dug in with hastily cast cannon at Raydaniyya, north of Cairo; the Ottomans turned his flank, took the city after days of street fighting, and hunted him down. Selim I had him hanged at the Bab Zuwayla in April 1517. Egypt became an Ottoman province and remained one until Bonaparte's landing in 1798.
entries.note: Ibn Iyas, day by day and shaken; the Ottoman chronicles. Winter and Levanoni (eds.), 'The Mamluks in Egyptian and Syrian Politics and Society' (2004), on the transition. Cross-references the Abbasid 945–1258 folio.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: A ruling class renewed by import every generation, the Abbasid caliph as a figurehead, four chief qadis, and the harshest phase of the dhimma

entries.label: The Mamluk system — a one-generation ruling caste
entries.hint: Political power was reserved to men bought as non-Muslim boys on the Qipchaq steppe or in the Caucasus, converted, raised in the Citadel barracks, and manumitted: only the foreign-born, slave-trained soldier could hold high military rank or the sultanate itself. Their own sons, the awlad al-nas, were barred from the elite. The aristocracy renewed itself by import every generation — a deliberately non-hereditary state.
entries.note: the institution is reconstructed above all by David Ayalon in a long series of articles (collected as 'Studies on the Mamluks of Egypt', 1977, and later volumes); al-Qalqashandi's 'Subh al-Asha' describes the ranks and offices from the inside. Cross-references the Abbasid 945–1258 and Ayyubid folios.

entries.label: Servant of the Two Sanctuaries
entries.hint: The Mamluk sultan took the title Servant of the Two Sanctuaries, appointed and deposed the Sharifs of Mecca, sent the covering (kiswa) for the Kaaba and grain for the Hijaz every year, and dispatched the Egyptian pilgrim caravan with its ceremonial litter, the mahmal. It made Cairo, not Baghdad or Damascus, the working political centre of Sunni Islam.
entries.note: Ibn Battuta and the pilgrimage accounts; Jomier, 'Le Mahmal et la caravane égyptienne des pèlerins de la Mecque' (1953); Meloy, 'Imperial Power and Maritime Trade: Mecca and Cairo in the Later Middle Ages' (2010).

entries.label: The Abbasid caliphate reinstalled in Cairo
entries.hint: Baybars received a fugitive uncle of the last Baghdad caliph, had him acclaimed as al-Mustansir, and thereafter each Mamluk sultan took his investiture from a powerless Abbasid kept at the Citadel. The line gave the sultanate a fig-leaf of legitimacy for 256 years, until Selim I carried the last Cairo caliph, al-Mutawakkil III, off to Istanbul.
entries.note: al-Maqrizi, 'Khitat'; the shadow caliphate in Holt, 'Some Observations on the Abbasid Caliphate of Cairo', BSOAS (1984). The later Ottoman claim to a transfer of the caliphate is a much later fabrication. Cross-references the Abbasid 945–1258 folio.

entries.label: The four chief qadis
entries.hint: Baybars replaced the single Shafi'i chief judge of Egypt with one chief qadi for each of the four Sunni law schools, giving all four equal official standing. The reform spread through the Sunni world and fixed the four-madhhab structure of Sunni law that survives today.
entries.note: al-Maqrizi; Escovitz, 'The Office of Qadi al-Qudat in Cairo under the Bahri Mamluks' (1984); Rapoport, 'Legal Diversity in the Age of Taqlid', Islamic Law and Society (2003).

entries.label: The iqta, the halqa and the rawk survey
entries.hint: The military land-assignment system reached its most elaborate form under the Qalawunids. Al-Nasir Muhammad's cadastral survey of 1315 (al-rawk al-Nasiri) redistributed the revenue of Egypt among the sultan and his emirs and cut the share of the halqa, the non-Mamluk cavalry, hastening its decline into a militia of tradesmen.
entries.note: Rabie, 'The Financial System of Egypt AH 564–741' (1972); Sato, 'State and Rural Society in Medieval Islam' (1997), on the rawk surveys.

entries.label: Government by military office
entries.hint: The state ran through a hierarchy of military-rank offices — the viceroy (na'ib al-saltana), the commander-in-chief (atabak al-asakir), the executive secretary (dawadar), the household steward (ustadar) — held by Mamluk emirs, with a parallel civilian bureaucracy of scribes, mostly Copts and awlad al-nas, doing the paperwork.
entries.note: al-Qalqashandi, 'Subh al-Asha' (1412), catalogues the whole apparatus; Ibn Fadl Allah al-Umari's 'al-Ta'rif' does the same a century earlier. Van Steenbergen, 'Order out of Chaos' (2006).

entries.label: The 1301 edict and the assault on the dhimma
entries.hint: Pressed by jurists and by mobs, al-Nasir Muhammad's government issued the harshest anti-dhimmi measures of medieval Egypt: Coptic and Jewish officials dismissed en masse, churches and synagogues closed, distinctive dress and the ghiyar rigidly enforced, repeated across the century (notably in 1321 and 1354). Forced conversion and the collapse of the Coptic scribal class followed.
entries.note: al-Maqrizi and the 'History of the Patriarchs'; the 1301 decree text partly preserved. el-Leithy, 'Coptic Culture and Conversion in Medieval Cairo 1293–1524' (PhD 2005); Little, 'Coptic Conversion to Islam under the Bahri Mamluks', BSOAS (1976). Cross-references the Ayyubid folio.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Cairo and Damascus as the capitals of Sunni learning after Baghdad, Ibn Taymiyya against the current, Sufism everywhere, and the definitive age of hadith scholarship

entries.label: The Jewish communities and the office of nagid
entries.hint: The Rabbanite and Karaite communities shrank with the general population and the anti-dhimmi pressure, but kept their institutions. The nagid, the head of the Jews recognised by the sultan, was often a physician at the Citadel and for several generations a descendant of Maimonides; the office lapsed around 1500.
entries.note: the tail of the Cairo Geniza (Goitein, 'A Mediterranean Society', 1967–93); the Maimonidean nagids in Ashtor, 'The Jews of Moslem Spain' notwithstanding — see rather his 'History of the Jews in Egypt and Syria under the Mamluks' (1944–70, Hebrew). Cross-references the Ayyubid folio.

entries.label: The twin capitals of Sunni learning
entries.hint: With Baghdad destroyed, the Mamluk cities became the centre of gravity of Sunni scholarship: hundreds of endowed madrasas and dar al-hadiths, the four law schools taught side by side, and a dense network of teaching licences (ijazas) that drew students from the Maghreb to India and made Cairo the place a Sunni scholar had to be seen.
entries.note: Berkey, 'The Transmission of Knowledge in Medieval Cairo' (1992); Chamberlain, 'Knowledge and Social Practice in Medieval Damascus 1190–1350' (1994).

entries.label: The tariqas and the age of the saint
entries.hint: Organised Sufism pervaded Mamluk society: the Shadhiliyya, whose founder's successor Ibn Ata Allah al-Iskandari wrote the 'Hikam', the most-read Sufi manual ever; the Rifaiyya and the Qadiriyya; and above all the cult of Ahmad al-Badawi of Tanta, whose annual mawlid drew tens of thousands and remains Egypt's largest religious festival.
entries.note: Ibn Ata Allah, 'al-Hikam' and 'Lataif al-Minan'; al-Munawi's later 'al-Kawakib al-Durriyya' (Sufi biographical dictionary). McGregor and Sabra (eds.), 'Le développement du soufisme en Égypte à l'époque mamelouke' (2006); Hofer, 'The Popularisation of Sufism in Ayyubid and Mamluk Egypt' (2015).

entries.label: The school of Ibn Arabi and the unity of being
entries.hint: Ibn Arabi's metaphysics of the unity of being was carried into the mainstream by his stepson al-Qunawi and a chain of commentators — al-Qashani, al-Qaysari — and systematised by al-Jili in 'The Universal Man' (al-Insan al-Kamil). It also drew sustained attack from Ibn Taymiyya and others; the argument over wahdat al-wujud runs through the whole period.
entries.note: al-Jili, 'al-Insan al-Kamil'; Chittick, 'The Sufi Path of Knowledge' (1989) and 'Faith and Practice of Islam' (1992). Knysh, 'Ibn Arabi in the Later Islamic Tradition' (1999), on the controversy. Cross-references the Abbasid 945–1258, Ayyubid and Al-Andalus 1031–1492 folios.

entries.label: Ibn Taymiyya
entries.hint: The Damascus Hanbali jurist campaigned against saint-cults, tomb-visitation, speculative theology and the philosophers, and issued the fatwas declaring armed jihad against the nominally-Muslim Ilkhanids licit. Tried and imprisoned repeatedly by his fellow ulama, he died in the citadel of Damascus in 1328. Marginal and much-condemned in his own time, his work became the fountainhead of later Salafism.
entries.note: Ibn Taymiyya's own vast corpus; the biography by his student Ibn Abd al-Hadi. Little, 'Did Ibn Taymiyya Have a Screw Loose?', Studia Islamica (1975); Bori and Rapoport (eds.), 'Ibn Taymiyya and His Times' (2010). Cross-references the Abbasid 945–1258 and Ayyubid folios.

entries.label: The definitive age of hadith scholarship
entries.hint: The Mamluk schools produced the standing apparatus of Sunni hadith study: al-Mizzi's dictionary of transmitters, al-Dhahabi's biographical history, and above all Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani's 'Fath al-Bari', the commentary on al-Bukhari that has never been superseded, followed by his students al-Sakhawi and the polymath al-Suyuti.
entries.note: Ibn Hajar, 'Fath al-Bari' and 'al-Isaba'; al-Sakhawi's memoir of his teacher, 'al-Jawahir wal-Durar'. Ozkan, and the studies in the 'Ibn Hajar' volume of the Oxford handbook tradition.

entries.label: The Coptic church retreats to the monasteries
entries.hint: Under fiscal pressure, mob violence and the edicts of 1301 and after, the Coptic community contracted sharply: the administrative families converted, Coptic ceased to be spoken, and the church's centre of gravity moved from the towns to the desert monasteries of Wadi Natrun and the Red Sea mountains, which carried the liturgical tradition through the lean centuries.
entries.note: the 'History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria' (contemporary, though thinner for this period); Swanson, 'The Coptic Papacy in Islamic Egypt' (2010); den Heijer and others. Cross-references the Ayyubid folio.

entries.label: The reading of the Quran systematised
entries.hint: Ibn al-Jazari of Damascus fixed the science of Quranic recitation: his works on the ten canonical readings and the chains of their transmission became, and remain, the standard reference, and he built a network of teaching institutions for reciters that reached from Damascus to Bursa to Shiraz.
entries.note: Ibn al-Jazari, 'al-Nashr fi al-Qiraat al-Ashr' and 'Ghayat al-Nihaya' (his own biographical dictionary of Quran reciters); the standard modern account in Nöldeke-Schwally's 'Geschichte des Qorans', updated.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The stone city of Cairo, the carved domes of the Circassian period, inlaid metal and enamelled glass, monumental Qurans, and the coffee-house epic

entries.label: Mamluk inlaid metalwork and the blazon
entries.hint: Brass basins, ewers, candlesticks and boxes inlaid with silver and gold, covered in bold thuluth inscriptions and, increasingly, the heraldic blazons of their owners — the cup of the cup-bearer, the pen-box of the secretary. The 'Baptistere de Saint Louis', signed by Muhammad ibn al-Zayn, is the masterpiece; lighter export versions later reached Venice.
entries.note: the Baptistere (Louvre); Ward, 'Islamic Metalwork' (1993); Mayer, 'Saracenic Heraldry' (1933), on the blazon system. Behrens-Abouseif, 'The Baptistere de Saint Louis' (forthcoming studies).

entries.label: Enamelled glass and its extinction
entries.hint: The gilded and polychrome-enamelled glass of Syria reached its height in the great mosque lamps endowed to Cairo madrasas. The craft died abruptly when Timur deported the Damascus glassmakers to Samarqand in 1401; Mamluk Egypt never recovered the technique, and Venice inherited the European market for enamelled glass.
entries.note: Carboni, 'Glass from Islamic Lands' (2001); the mosque lamps of Sultan Hasan and others, many now dispersed to museums. The Timur deportation is in Ibn Taghribirdi and the Timurid sources.

entries.label: The stone city of the Mamluks
entries.hint: The Mamluk emirs competed in stone: Qalawun's madrasa-hospital-mausoleum (1284–85), the colossal madrasa-mosque of Sultan Hasan (1356–63), and hundreds of smaller complexes lining the main streets, each with a domed founder's tomb turned to face the passer-by. The tomb-madrasa, inherited from the Ayyubids, became the defining Cairo monument.
entries.note: Behrens-Abouseif, 'Cairo of the Mamluks: A History of the Architecture and its Culture' (2007), is the standard survey; the foundation inscriptions are primary documents in themselves. Cross-references the Ayyubid folio.

entries.label: Shadow theatre, the coffee-house epic and the Nights
entries.hint: Ibn Daniyal wrote three shadow-play scripts in Cairo around 1300 — bawdy, satirical, the only medieval Arabic drama texts to survive. In the same centuries the oral epic cycles took lasting shape — the 'Sirat Baybars', built around the Mamluk founder himself, recited to the rabab — and the 'Thousand and One Nights' reached something close to its familiar form in Mamluk Syria, where the oldest substantial manuscript was copied.
entries.note: Ibn Daniyal, 'Tayf al-Khayal', ed. and trans. Corrao and others; the Galland manuscript of the 'Nights' (14th–15th c. Syrian, BnF); Irwin, 'The Arabian Nights: A Companion' (1994); Lyons, 'The Arabian Epic' (1995).

entries.label: The monumental Quran and the Cairo school of illumination
entries.hint: Sultans and emirs endowed their madrasas with huge multi-volume Qurans in bold muhaqqaq script with gold-and-blue geometric frontispieces. The calligraphers Ibn al-Wahid and Sandal and the Cairo and Damascus ateliers set a standard of book production that later Ilkhanid and Timurid patrons deliberately imitated.
entries.note: James, 'Qurans of the Mamluks' (1988), the catalogue and study; the endowed Qurans of Baybars al-Jashnakir and Sultan Sha'ban survive.

entries.label: Encyclopedias, anthologies and the chancery arts
entries.hint: The age's characteristic literary form was the vast compilation: al-Nuwayri's thirty-one-volume 'Nihayat al-Arab', al-Umari's geography 'Masalik al-Absar', al-Qalqashandi's fourteen-volume chancery manual 'Subh al-Asha', and al-Safadi's biographical dictionaries. Adab became curatorial — the ordering and preservation of a huge inherited tradition.
entries.note: the works themselves, all edited and in print; Muhanna, 'The World in a Book: al-Nuwayri and the Islamic Encyclopedic Tradition' (2018).

entries.label: The carved stone domes of the Circassian period
entries.hint: Cairo's masons developed a way of cutting complex interlacing geometric and then floral patterns into the exterior masonry of large stone domes — attempted at this scale nowhere else — culminating in the domes of Qaytbay's Northern Cemetery complex of 1472–74, often called the most perfectly resolved Mamluk building.
entries.note: Behrens-Abouseif (2007); the technical study in Kessler, 'The Carved Masonry Domes of Mediaeval Cairo' (1976).

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Ibn Khaldun's science of society, the Egyptian school of historians, Ibn al-Nafis and the lungs, Ibn al-Shatir and the planets, and the dictionaries

entries.label: Ibn al-Nafis and the pulmonary transit of the blood
entries.hint: Working in Ayyubid and then Mamluk Cairo, the physician Ibn al-Nafis argued in his commentary on Avicenna's 'Canon' that blood passes from the right side of the heart to the left through the lungs, not through invisible pores in the dividing wall — the pulmonary circulation, three centuries before Servetus and Harvey. He was chief physician of the great Mansuri hospital.
entries.note: the 'Sharh Tashrih al-Qanun', the relevant passage published by Meyerhof in 1935; the debate over transmission to Renaissance Europe (via the Latin of Andrea Alpago). Cross-references the Ayyubid folio's medicine entry.

entries.label: The Lisan al-Arab and the Qamus
entries.hint: Two of the largest Arabic dictionaries ever compiled were finished under the Mamluks: Ibn Manzur's twenty-volume 'Lisan al-Arab' (d. 1311), which gathered the whole earlier lexical tradition into one alphabetical work, and al-Fayruzabadi's more compact 'al-Qamus al-Muhit' (d. 1415), the standard desk reference for the next five centuries.
entries.note: both in print in many editions; the lexicographical tradition surveyed in Haywood, 'Arabic Lexicography' (1960).

entries.label: The muwaqqit and the mathematics of worship
entries.hint: The Mamluk mosques employed salaried astronomers, muwaqqits, to fix the five daily prayer times and the direction of Mecca. Al-Khalili's Damascus tables gave the qibla for every degree of latitude and longitude, and the astrolabic quadrant, a Mamluk simplification, made the calculation portable. Religious need sustained a genuine research programme in applied mathematics.
entries.note: David A. King, 'In Synchrony with the Heavens: Studies in Astronomical Timekeeping and Instrumentation in Medieval Islamic Civilization' (2004–05); al-Khalili's tables analysed there.

entries.label: The plague treatises
entries.hint: The Black Death forced Muslim scholars to write about epidemic disease: works debating whether plague spread by contagion or came as divine visitation, whether flight from a stricken town was permitted, and what remedies helped. Ibn Hajar and al-Suyuti both wrote plague tracts; the genre records the intellectual effort to explain a catastrophe that killed a third of the people.
entries.note: Dols, 'The Black Death in the Middle East' (1977), catalogues and analyses the treatise literature; Ibn Hajar's 'Badhl al-Maun fi Fadl al-Taun'.

entries.label: Ibn al-Shatir and late Islamic astronomy
entries.hint: The timekeeper of the Umayyad Mosque in Damascus built planetary models that eliminated the Ptolemaic equant using only combinations of uniform circular motion — models mathematically identical to those Copernicus would publish in 1543. His work shows Islamic theoretical astronomy still advancing a century after the Maragha observatory.
entries.note: Ibn al-Shatir, 'Nihayat al-Sul'; Roberts, 'The Solar and Lunar Theory of Ibn al-Shatir', Isis (1957), and Kennedy's studies; Saliba, 'Islamic Science and the Making of the European Renaissance' (2007).

entries.label: Ibn Khaldun and the science of society
entries.hint: The Tunisian jurist-historian settled in Mamluk Cairo in 1382, taught, and served six times as Maliki chief qadi. There he completed the 'Muqaddima' — his theory of asabiyya, or group solidarity, the cyclical rise and decay of dynasties, an early analysis of the economics of taxation and labour, and a withering critique of how historians handle evidence. In 1401 he was let down over the wall of besieged Damascus to negotiate with Timur.
entries.note: the 'Muqaddima', trans. Rosenthal (1958); Ibn Khaldun's autobiography 'al-Ta'rif'. Fischel, 'Ibn Khaldun in Egypt' (1967) and 'Ibn Khaldun and Tamerlane' (1952); Irwin, 'Ibn Khaldun: An Intellectual Biography' (2018).

entries.label: The Egyptian school of historians
entries.hint: Mamluk Egypt produced a continuous, self-aware tradition of urban history: al-Maqrizi's topography of Cairo ('al-Khitat') and his chronicle 'al-Suluk', Ibn Taghribirdi's 'al-Nujum al-Zahira', al-Sakhawi's biographical dictionary of the fifteenth century, and Ibn Iyas, whose year-by-year chronicle is an eyewitness account of the Ottoman conquest.
entries.note: all edited and largely translated; al-Maqrizi's moralising decline-frame and nostalgia for the Bahri period colour the 'Khitat' and must be read for it (Bauden's 'al-Maqrizi Project'). Ibn Iyas is partisan but on the spot for 1501–17.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: The spice-transit monopoly and the Karimi, Barsbay's crown monopolies, the Black Death, the copper inflation, the slave supply, and the Portuguese shock

entries.label: The transit trade and the Karimi merchants
entries.hint: Egypt monopolised the flow of pepper, spices and Asian goods from the Indian Ocean through Aden and the Red Sea to Alexandria, where the Italians bought them. The Karimi — a corporation of perhaps fifty great families — financed the trade, banked the sultans, ransomed captives, and endowed madrasas of their own.
entries.note: Goitein and Friedman, 'India Traders of the Middle Ages' (2008); Ashtor, 'The Karimi Merchants', JRAS (1956), with the corrections in Fischel and in Wing. Cross-references the Ayyubid and Abbasid 945–1258 folios.

entries.label: The slave trade — the Black Sea, the Caucasus and Cairo
entries.hint: The regime was fed by a continuous import of enslaved children: Qipchaq Turks shipped from the Golden Horde's ports through Genoese Caffa and across the Bosphorus by treaty with Byzantium in the Bahri period; then, as the Ottomans closed the straits and taste shifted, Circassians brought overland from the Caucasus. Genoese and Venetian shippers carried much of the traffic; the Cairo market, the Suq al-Nakhkhasin, was its clearing house.
entries.note: the Byzantine treaty of 1281 and the Venetian and Genoese material in Ashtor, 'Levant Trade in the Later Middle Ages' (1983); Amitai and Cluse (eds.), 'Slavery and the Slave Trade in the Eastern Mediterranean c.1000–1500' (2017). Cross-references the Abbasid 945–1258 and Ayyubid folios.

entries.label: The Venetian and Genoese factories
entries.hint: Venice, Genoa and Catalonia kept fortified trading compounds (funduqs), consuls and resident colonies at Alexandria and Damascus, and the Venetian state ran scheduled convoys of great galleys (the muda) to Alexandria and Beirut every year. Egypt sent out cotton, spices, alum and sugar against silver, woollens, metals and arms.
entries.note: Ashtor, 'Levant Trade in the Later Middle Ages' (1983); the Venetian Senate's 'Deliberazioni' and the consular records; Christ, 'Trading Conflicts: Venetian Merchants and Mamluk Officials in Late Medieval Alexandria' (2012). Cross-references the Ayyubid folio.

entries.label: The Black Death and the recurring plague
entries.hint: The first wave of 1347–49 killed perhaps a third of the people of Egypt and Syria; some fifty further outbreaks followed to 1517. The Mamluk state — dependent on a centrally managed irrigation system and a dense tax base — was hit harder and recovered less than western Europe: villages were abandoned, canals silted, and per-capita revenue never returned to its pre-plague level.
entries.note: Dols, 'The Black Death in the Middle East' (1977); Borsch, 'The Black Death in Egypt and England: A Comparative Study' (2005), for the irrigation-collapse thesis; the demographic debate continues (Borsch and Sabraa, 2016).

entries.label: The rural crisis — iqta, Bedouin and shrinking cultivation
entries.hint: After the plague the cultivated area of Egypt contracted sharply. Emirs milked their iqtas for short-term cash, the irrigation corvee broke down, and Arab tribes — the Hawwara in the south above all — moved into the vacuum as tax-farmers and raiders. Egypt's agrarian output around 1500 stood well below its thirteenth-century level.
entries.note: Borsch, 'The Black Death in Egypt and England' (2005); Petry, 'Fractionalized Estates in a Centralized Regime', JESHO (1998); Garcin on the Hawwara and Upper Egypt.

entries.label: The copper inflation and the debased dirham
entries.hint: The silver dirham effectively vanished from circulation; the state flooded the market with copper fulus, and prices in copper terms rose several-fold within a generation. Al-Maqrizi's tract 'Ighathat al-Umma bi-Kashf al-Ghumma' blames the crisis on monetary mismanagement, official corruption and the plague — one of the earliest analytical works on inflation.
entries.note: al-Maqrizi, 'Ighathat al-Umma', trans. Allouche as 'Mamluk Economics' (1994); Bacharach, 'Circassian Monetary Policy: Copper', JESHO (1976).

entries.label: Barsbay's monopolies and the ruin of the Karimi
entries.hint: Barsbay forced first sugar, then pepper and spices, through crown monopolies: merchants had to sell to the sultan at a fixed low price and buy from him at a fixed high one. It filled the treasury for a decade and destroyed the Karimi as an independent force, leaving the transit economy dependent on the state and exposed.
entries.note: al-Maqrizi (a hostile contemporary witness); Darrag, 'L'Égypte sous le règne de Barsbay' (1961); Wing, 'The Karimi Merchants of Cairo', Mamluk Studies Review (2004).

entries.label: The Portuguese and the collapse of the spice revenue
entries.hint: Vasco da Gama's Cape route let Portugal buy pepper at the source and sell it in Lisbon below the Alexandria price. Within fifteen years the Venetian spice purchases at Alexandria had fallen by more than half, gutting the customs revenue on which the late Mamluk treasury depended — a fiscal wound the Ottoman conquest merely finished.
entries.note: the Venetian purchase figures in Lane, 'Venice and History' (1966); Wake, 'The Changing Pattern of Europe's Pepper and Spice Imports', Journal of European Economic History (1979). Cross-references the Ayyubid folio.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The refusal of the hand-gun, the science of horsemanship, the relay post and the pigeon service, block-printed amulets, and the sugar works

entries.label: Furusiyya — the science of horsemanship
entries.hint: Mamluk training was codified in a large technical literature — riding, lance and sabre technique, mounted archery, cavalry evolutions, veterinary care — practised in the great hippodromes below the Citadel. It was at once a military system and the cultural core of the ruling caste's identity.
entries.note: the furusiyya manuals surveyed in al-Sarraf's studies and in the exhibition catalogue 'Furusiyya' (1996); many are illustrated. Nettles, 'Mamluk Cavalry Practices' (2001).

entries.label: The relay post, the pigeon service and the signal towers
entries.hint: Baybars rebuilt a state relay-post (barid) with staging stables from Cairo to the Euphrates, a carrier-pigeon service with registered birds and recorded pedigrees, and a chain of fire-and-smoke towers that could pass warning of a Mongol river crossing from the frontier to Cairo within a day. Rapid communication was a strategic technology of the Mongol frontier.
entries.note: Sauvaget, 'La poste aux chevaux dans l'empire des Mamelouks' (1941); al-Qalqashandi describes the barid and the pigeon post in detail; Silverstein, 'Postal Systems in the Pre-Modern Islamic World' (2007).

entries.label: Sugar, saltpetre and the chemical trades
entries.loc: the Egyptian Delta and Nile valley
entries.hint: The Egyptian sugar industry ran large mechanised presses and multi-stage boiling and refining houses producing loaf sugar and molasses for export. The same technical base supported saltpetre extraction for gunpowder and a distillation industry for rosewater and medicines. The sugar works decayed with the rural economy after 1400.
entries.note: Ashtor, 'Levant Trade' (1983), and his article on the Levantine sugar industry, JESHO (1977); the archaeology of the Egyptian and Syrian mills.

entries.label: Block-printed amulets
entries.hint: Craftsmen in Mamluk Egypt printed miniature Quranic texts and prayers from carved wood or metal blocks onto paper strips (tarsh), sold as amulets — a working block-printing technology two centuries before Gutenberg, though it stayed confined to charms and never challenged the hand copyist. Almost all surviving specimens are Mamluk-era.
entries.note: Bulliet, 'Medieval Arabic Tarsh: A Forgotten Chapter in the History of Printing', JAOS (1987); Schaefer, 'Enigmatic Charms: Medieval Arabic Block Printed Amulets' (2006).

entries.label: Gunpowder and the Mamluk resistance to firearms
entries.hint: The Mamluks used siege cannon from the late fourteenth century and kept an artillery park, but the cavalry corps despised the hand-gun as unchivalrous and unfit for a horseman. Al-Ghawri's late attempt to raise a salaried arquebus corps (al-tabaqa al-khamisa) from non-Mamluks was resented and came far too late to answer the Ottoman infantry firepower at Marj Dabiq.
entries.note: Ayalon, 'Gunpowder and Firearms in the Mamluk Kingdom: A Challenge to a Mediaeval Society' (1956), the classic study; the debate revisited in the 'Mamluk Studies Review' and by Petry.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: The Golden Horde alliance, peace with the converted Ilkhanate, treaties with Latin Christendom, Ibn Battuta, Mansa Musa, and the embassies from the Indian Ocean

entries.label: The Golden Horde alliance against the Ilkhanate
entries.hint: Baybars allied with Berke, the first Muslim khan of the Golden Horde, against their common enemy the Ilkhanate; the two powers exchanged embassies across the Byzantine straits for sixty years. The alliance kept open the Black Sea route that supplied the Mamluk army with slave recruits.
entries.note: Ibn Abd al-Zahir preserves the diplomatic correspondence; Amitai-Preiss, 'Mongols and Mamluks' (1995); Favereau, 'The Horde: How the Mongols Changed the World' (2021), on the Berke-Baybars axis.

entries.label: The diplomacy that replaced the Crusades
entries.hint: With Outremer gone, the Mamluks dealt with Latin Christendom through treaties — with Aragon, Genoa, Venice, Cyprus and the Hospitallers of Rhodes — covering trade, piracy, the ransom of captives, and, as a Mamluk lever, access for Christian pilgrims to Jerusalem, which the sultan taxed and could close at will.
entries.note: Holt, 'Early Mamluk Diplomacy 1260–1290: Treaties of Baybars and Qalawun with Christian Rulers' (1995); the Aragonese material in Atiya, 'Egypt and Aragon' (1938). Cross-references the Ayyubid folio.

entries.label: European eyes on Egypt
entries.hint: A steady stream of Latin visitors left accounts: pilgrims bound for Sinai and Jerusalem (Frescobaldi, Arnold von Harff), Venetian and Genoese consuls, and the authors of crusade-recovery treatises like Marino Sanudo, who proposed strangling the sultanate with a naval blockade of the spice trade. Their reports are a major source and shaped how Europe pictured the Mamluk state.
entries.note: Sanudo, 'Liber Secretorum Fidelium Crucis' (c.1321); the pilgrim narratives collected in the 'Palestine Pilgrims' Text Society' volumes; Arnold von Harff's illustrated account (c.1497).

entries.label: Making peace with the Mongols
entries.hint: After sixty years of frontier war, al-Nasir Muhammad and the Ilkhan Abu Said signed a formal peace. The Ilkhanate had by then converted to Islam; embassies and trade resumed, and the Euphrates settled as a recognised border until the Ilkhanate dissolved in the 1330s.
entries.note: al-Maqrizi and al-Nuwayri; the 1323 treaty in the context of the Ilkhanate's Islamisation (Amitai, 'The Resolution of the Mongol-Mamluk War', in Amitai and Biran (eds.), 'Mongols, Turks and Others', 2005).

entries.label: Mansa Musa's hajj and the Cairo gold market
entries.hint: The ruler of Mali crossed Egypt on pilgrimage with a caravan carrying so much gold that, al-Umari was told a decade later, the Cairo price of gold had still not recovered. The episode fixed Mali on European maps and marks the height of the trans-Saharan gold trade that fed the Mediterranean economy.
entries.note: al-Umari, 'Masalik al-Absar' (he interviewed Cairenes who had met the Malian party); Levtzion and Hopkins, 'Corpus of Early Arabic Sources for West African History' (1981).

entries.label: Ibn Battuta in the Mamluk lands
entries.hint: The Tangier traveller passed through Alexandria, Cairo, Damascus and the Hijaz on his way east, and his 'Rihla' — dictated decades later at the Marinid court — is one of the fullest descriptions of Mamluk cities, the pilgrimage routes and the scholarly world at their height.
entries.note: the 'Rihla', trans. Gibb and Beckingham (1958–2000); the text was shaped by the court secretary Ibn Juzayy and embellished — read with Waines, 'The Odyssey of Ibn Battuta' (2010), and the sceptical literature.

entries.label: Embassies from the Indian Ocean and Ming China
entries.hint: As protector of Mecca the Mamluk sultan received missions from the sultanates of Gujarat and Bengal, from Vijayanagara and Ceylon, and — through Aden — from the Ming treasure fleets of Zheng He, which reached the Red Sea in the 1410s and 1430s and carried Mamluk and Meccan envoys back to China.
entries.note: the Chinese record in the 'Ming Shi' and Ma Huan's 'Yingya Shenglan'; the Mamluk side thinner (al-Maqrizi notes the 1432 mission). Meloy, 'Imperial Power and Maritime Trade' (2010); Sen, and Church on Zheng He at Aden.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The Mongols stopped at the Euphrates, the Latin East liquidated, Cairo the greatest city west of China, the Black Death, and the double blow of the Portuguese and the Ottomans

entries.label: The Mongols are stopped
entries.hint: Ayn Jalut and the sixty-year defence of the Euphrates line preserved a major independent Islamic power in the west at the very moment the eastern Islamic world fell under Mongol rule. Egypt and Muslim Syria were the part of the Dar al-Islam the Mongols never took — and the base from which Sunni Islam and the Arabic learned tradition carried on.
entries.note: Amitai-Preiss, 'Mongols and Mamluks' (1995). Cross-references the Abbasid 945–1258 and Ayyubid folios.

entries.label: The Latin East is liquidated
entries.hint: The fall of Acre ended the crusader states. There would be crusade plans, and Cypriot and Rhodian raids, for another two centuries, but never again a Latin territorial foothold on the Syrian mainland. The Mamluks had removed the western beachhead in the Levant.
entries.note: Prawer, 'The Latin Kingdom of Jerusalem' (1972); Housley, 'The Later Crusades 1274–1580' (1992), on what came after. Cross-references the Ayyubid folio.

entries.label: Cairo, the greatest city west of China
entries.hint: With Baghdad in ruins, Mamluk Cairo — perhaps half a million people before the plague — was the largest city in the Mediterranean and Middle Eastern world: seat of the caliph, funnel of the spice trade, and the leading centre of Sunni learning. The Black Death ended that primacy, and it never fully returned.
entries.note: Raymond, 'Cairo' (Eng. trans. 2000); the population estimates debated (Dols; Russell). Ibn Khaldun and al-Umari both call Cairo the metropolis of the world.

entries.label: The Black Death on the western arm of the pandemic
entries.hint: Plague reached Alexandria by ship in 1347 and swept Egypt and Syria over the next two years. On one influential reading, the Mamluk state's dependence on a centralised, corvee-maintained irrigation system meant the demographic collapse did lasting structural damage that the more decentralised agriculture of western Europe escaped.
entries.note: Dols, 'The Black Death in the Middle East' (1977); Borsch, 'The Black Death in Egypt and England' (2005). al-Maqrizi's day-by-day account is the fullest narrative source for any society in the first wave.

entries.label: The spice route goes around Africa
entries.hint: The Portuguese Cape route broke the Red Sea and Alexandria spice monopoly that had underwritten Egyptian state finance since the Fatimids. The Mamluk naval counter-effort failed at Diu in 1509, and the customs revenue collapsed on the eve of the Ottoman conquest.
entries.note: Casale, 'The Ottoman Age of Exploration' (2010); Wake (1979) on the pepper figures. Cross-references the Ayyubid folio's Red Sea entries.

entries.label: The cavalry state and the gunpowder empire
entries.hint: The Mamluk Sultanate is the textbook case of a mounted-warrior state overrun by a gunpowder empire: the Ottomans combined massed arquebusiers, chained field artillery and a disciplined standing infantry that the Mamluk cavalry ethos could not match. How much was technology and how much the defection of Khayrbak and Janbirdi al-Ghazali is argued still.
entries.note: Ayalon, 'Gunpowder and Firearms in the Mamluk Kingdom' (1956); the revisionist weighting of politics over technology in Petry, 'Protectors or Praetorians?' (1994).

entries.label: The Ottoman conquest and the end of medieval Egypt
entries.hint: Selim I's victories at Marj Dabiq and Raydaniyya made Egypt, Syria and the Hijaz Ottoman provinces and carried the last Cairo Abbasid to Istanbul. Egypt would not again be ruled from Cairo by a native regime until the twentieth century; the Mamluk households survived as a provincial governing class until Muhammad Ali destroyed them in 1811.
entries.note: Ibn Iyas; Winter, 'Egyptian Society under Ottoman Rule 1517–1798' (1992); Hathaway, 'The Politics of Households in Ottoman Egypt' (1997), on the survival of the Mamluk system. Cross-references the Abbasid 945–1258 folio.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: The making of a Mamluk, the great ladies of the Citadel, the sons barred from power, the eunuchs, the beloved in the biographical dictionaries, and plague at eye level

entries.label: The making of a Mamluk
entries.hint: A boy of eight to twelve, bought on the Qipchaq steppe or in the Caucasus, was shipped to Cairo, housed in the Citadel barracks under a eunuch tutor, taught Arabic, the Quran and horsemanship, converted to Islam, and manumitted on graduation — thereafter bound for life to his master and his barracks cohort by ties that structured all Mamluk politics. The luckiest rose to emir, or to sultan.
entries.note: Ayalon, 'The Mamluk Novice' and 'L'esclavage du Mamelouk' (1951), reconstructed from the chronicles and the furusiyya and administrative literature. Cross-references the Abbasid 945–1258 and Ayyubid folios.

entries.label: The great ladies of the Citadel
entries.hint: From Shajar al-Durr onward, the wives, mothers and daughters of sultans — the khawand — controlled large fortunes, founded and administered mosques, madrasas and mausolea, brokered marriages and successions, and occasionally ran the government behind a child sultan. Their endowment deeds are among the best evidence anywhere for elite women's economic power in the medieval Islamic world.
entries.note: the surviving waqf documents (Fernandes; Behrens-Abouseif); Petry, 'Class Solidarity versus Gender Gain: Women as Custodians of Property in Later Medieval Egypt', in Keddie and Baron (eds.) (1991). Cross-references the Ayyubid folio.

entries.label: The eunuchs of the Citadel and the Prophet's tomb
entries.hint: Eunuchs — enslaved and castrated outside the empire, then trained at the centre — were the tutors who raised the boy-Mamluks, the guardians of the harem and the treasury, senior military officers, and the keepers of the Prophet's mosque in Medina. They formed a recognised third category with access to spaces closed to other men.
entries.note: Ayalon, 'Eunuchs, Caliphs and Sultans: A Study in Power Relationships' (1999); Marmon, 'Eunuchs and Sacred Boundaries in Islamic Society' (1995), on the tomb eunuchs of Medina.

entries.label: Household slavery and the racial hierarchy
entries.hint: Below the military slaves were the far more numerous household slaves — concubines, wet-nurses, cooks, water-carriers, field workers — and a clear status ranking by origin: Turkish and Circassian at the top, then Ethiopian, then sub-Saharan African at the bottom, doing the heaviest work. Manumission was a routine act of piety and a common clause of wills.
entries.note: the tail of the Geniza and the Arabic manumission deeds; Marmon (ed.), 'Slavery in the Islamic Middle East' (1999); Perry, 'The Daily Life of Slaves and the Global Reach of Slavery in Medieval Egypt' (PhD 2014). Cross-references the Ayyubid folio.

entries.label: The beloved in Mamluk letters
entries.hint: The biographical dictionaries and poetry anthologies of the period are full of the love of men for beautiful youths — al-Safadi wrote both verse on the theme and a treatise, and the anecdote collections treat it as an ordinary feature of scholarly life — set against the flat prohibition of the act by the jurists. References to women's same-sex relations (sahq) appear in the medical and adab literature.
entries.note: al-Safadi, 'Law'at al-Shaki' and the 'Husn al-Tawassul'; the material surveyed in Wright and Rowson (eds.), 'Homoeroticism in Classical Arabic Literature' (1997), and El-Rouayheb, 'Before Homosexuality in the Arab-Islamic World 1500–1800' (2005). Cross-references the Ayyubid and Abbasid 945–1258 folios.

entries.label: The awlad al-nas — the sons who could not inherit
entries.hint: The children of Mamluks, born Muslim and free, were barred by the logic of the system from the military elite their fathers had held. They became the scholars, historians, poets, Sufi shaykhs and bureaucrats of Mamluk society — a whole cultured class defined by its exclusion from power. The historian Ibn Taghribirdi was one of them.
entries.note: Haarmann, 'Joseph's Law: The Careers and Activities of Mamluk Descendants before the Ottoman Conquest', in Philipp and Haarmann (eds.), 'The Mamluks in Egyptian Politics and Society' (1998).

entries.label: Plague at eye level
entries.hint: The chroniclers counted the dead by the day — al-Maqrizi records the biers backed up at the mosques, the mass graves, whole streets of Cairo emptied, entire households gone, the soaring price of a gravedigger and a coffin. The recurring plague is the best-documented lived experience of catastrophe in the medieval Islamic world.
entries.note: al-Maqrizi, 'Suluk', and Ibn Iyas for the later waves; Dols, 'The Black Death in the Middle East' (1977), ch. 5, on the social response.
